items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.

items.title: ROCE compares like with like across firm sizes
items.claim: A firm has operating profit of £2 million, total assets of £15 million and current liabilities of £5 million. What is ROCE?
items.reveal_title: Operating profit divided by capital employed
items.reveal:
Capital employed = total assets - current liabilities = £15m - £5m = £10m. ROCE = £2m / £10m = 20%.

ROCE is the most commonly cited single profitability measure in UK A-level. It is benchmarked against the cost of capital — if a firm consistently earns less than its weighted cost of capital, it is destroying shareholder value. UK FTSE 100 firms have averaged 10-15% ROCE over the last decade.
items.why: Absolute profit figures don't tell you whether capital was well used. A £2m profit from £10m of capital is 20%; the same profit from £100m of capital is 2%.

items.title: Most mergers and acquisitions destroy shareholder value
items.claim: Multiple long-run studies of M&A outcomes (KPMG, Bain, Harvard Business Review reviews) report what share of deals fail to create value for the acquiring firm's shareholders?
items.reveal:
KPMG's recurring M&A studies, Bain & Company's analyses, and Roger Martin's 2016 HBR piece 'M&A: The One Thing You Need to Get Right' all converge: 70-90% of acquisitions fail to deliver the anticipated synergies, often because the acquirer overpays.

Specific failures: AOL-Time Warner (2000, $165bn), Daimler-Chrysler (1998), Quaker-Snapple (1994), Microsoft-Nokia (2014). The 'winner's curse' (Thaler, 1988) explains why competitive bidding tends to produce winners who overestimated.

Organic growth tends to deliver more predictable returns but at a slower pace.
items.why: M&A is one of the most-used growth strategies and one of the worst-performing. The gap between expected and actual synergies is systematically positive.
